newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Ethiopia sees record coffee exports in 1996/97.
newsitem.headline: Ethiopia sees record coffee exports in 1996/97.

text.p: Ethiopian coffee industry officials on Monday forecast a bumper crop in the 1996/97 fiscal year and said exports would reach a record 108,000 tonnes.

They told Reuters in the capital Addis Ababa that drought sweeping much of Eastern Africa -- and which has cut production in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania -- had not affected Ethiopia's key coffee growing areas which continued to enjoy good rains.
"Good rains and better technology applied in coffee growing areas has helped to increase the volume of production," said Aster Estifanos of the Ethiopia Tea and Coffee Authority.

Aster said coffee supply from regions to the central market in Addis Ababa in the last seven months (July-January) had topped 80,000 tonnes compared to 56,000 tonnes in the same period in the previous year.
Aster, the Authority's head of planning, said Ethiopia had already exported 48,300 tonnes of the planned 108,000 tonnes of coffee in those seven months and earned around $120 million.
Ethiopia's coffee year is October/September but Aster's computations were based on the fiscal year July/June.
She said Ethiopia's earnings from coffee exports in 1996/97 were expected to rise because of better international market prices and strict control in the quality of exportable coffee.
A sizable volume of Ethiopia's coffee for exports this year would be washed coffee that fetches better price in the world market, she told Reuters in an interview.
She rejected reports from other local and regional coffee industry sources that coffee production in Ethiopia would be less than the annual average 250,000 tonnes due to drought.
"Ethiopia's coffee crop has not been affected by drought. In fact good rains prevailing in the country promises bumper harvest," Aster said but gave no specific forecast.
Ethiopia is Africa's third largest producer of coffee after Uganda and Ivory Coast. Neighbouring Kenya is Africa's fifth largest producer and drought now threatens its production.
Coffee is Ethiopia's main export commodity and accounts for about 60 percent of the country's hard currency earnings.
Ethiopia exported 102,000 tonnes of coffee in 1995/96 and earned $279.5 million -- lower than the $300.9 million it received for exporting 78,420 tonnes of coffee in 1994/95.
Its earnings in 1995/96 were undermined by declining global coffee prices in that year.
Aster confirmed Ethiopia would participate at a speciality coffee conference in the U.S. in April as part of its strategy to promote prime coffee varieties on the global market.
Ethiopia will also attend a "Speciality comes to London" coffee conference in October 1997, Aster said.
